paragraphs: In the years following a large volcanic eruption, the sulfur particles hurled into the upper atmosphere scatter sunlight and cool the surface of the planet by a fraction of a degree. Trees in cold regions are sensitive to such cooling, and their annual rings can record it: a ring that is unusually narrow or shows frost damage often marks a cool summer. Researchers who compare ring records from distant forests have found that several of the narrowest rings of the past millennium coincide with eruptions known from ice cores. Not every eruption leaves such a trace, however, and some narrow rings correspond to no known eruption at all. The method is therefore best used to corroborate dates established by other means, rather than as an independent clock for volcanic activity.
